title: Gabriel
def: The angel who brings God’s revelation to the prophets; Muslims believe he brought the Quran to Muhammad.
what: The Quran names Gabriel as the one who brought the Quran down “upon your heart” (2:97) and as “the Trustworthy Spirit” (26:193). Commentators identify him with the “Holy Spirit” (rūḥ al-qudus) who strengthened Jesus (2:87, 16:102). The Prophet saw him in his angelic form twice (53:5–18, 81:23). In the hadith of Gabriel he came in the form of a man to ask the Prophet about Islam, faith and excellence.
sources: Gabriel’s role in the Bible is the same: he announces to Zechariah the birth of John and to Mary the birth of Jesus (Luke 1). Khadija’s test of him, by asking the Prophet to tell her when he came and then uncovering herself, is related in Ibn Ishaq as a sign that the visitor was an angel.

title: Gambling
def: The Quran forbids gambling with intoxicants and idols as “an abomination of Satan’s work” (5:90).
what: “They ask you about intoxicants and gambling. Say: in them is great sin and some benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit” (2:219). “Satan only wishes to cause enmity and hatred between you through intoxicants and gambling, and to turn you from the remembrance of God” (5:91). The Prophet said that whoever says to his friend “come, let me gamble with you” should give charity (Sahih al-Bukhari), as expiation for the invitation.

title: Geiger, Abraham
def: A German rabbi (1810–1874), founder of Reform Judaism, who wrote in 1833 that the Quran drew on Jewish sources.
what: Abraham Geiger’s prize essay Was hat Mohammed aus dem Judenthume aufgenommen? (1833) collected parallels between the Quran and Jewish writings, and began a long tradition of Western scholarship tracing the Quran’s content to earlier sources.
sources: Muslims respond that the Quran itself says it confirms the earlier scriptures (2:41, 3:3), that it tells shared stories because it comes from the same God, and that it is no surprise that a revelation to a people near Jews and Christians should speak of Abraham and Moses. Whether one accepts the claim depends on what one thinks of the origin of the Quran.

title: Genetics and heredity
def: Hadith speak of children’s resemblance to parents and of a “vein” of ancestry, in the language of the time.
what: The Companion Abdullah ibn Salam asked the Prophet why a child resembles its father or its mother, and he answered that if the man’s fluid prevails the child resembles him, and if the woman’s, her (Sahih al-Bukhari). A man whose wife bore a dark child asked whether to disown it, and the Prophet asked about his camels, and whether any was grey; “perhaps a vein drew it”, he said, “perhaps your son’s vein drew him” (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim).
sources: Muslim scholars read the first as an observation about the dominance of one parent’s traits, in the terms available then. The second sets out heredity across generations, and the Prophet’s point was that the child was not to be disowned on appearance. Neither is presented as a lesson in genetics.

title: Genocide
def: Islamic law forbids killing non-combatants; genocide by any ruler, Muslim or not, is condemned by its standard.
what: The Quran says that whoever kills a person “other than for murder or corruption in the land” is as if he had killed all mankind (5:32). The Prophet forbade killing women, children and the old, and the early caliphs repeated it to their armies. The massacre of Armenians in 1915–16 was carried out by the Ottoman government of the Committee of Union and Progress, a secular nationalist party, and many Muslim families and some officials sheltered Armenians at risk to themselves.
sources: Mass killing has been done in many cultures. Muslims were the victims at Srebrenica in 1995 and in Myanmar since 2017, and others have been victims of Muslims. This site discusses the case of Banu Qurayza in its own entry.

title: Ghoul
def: The ghoul of Arabian folklore is not an Islamic belief; a hadith denies it.
what: The Prophet is reported to have said: “There is no contagion, no bad omen, no owl, no ghoul (lā ghūl)” (Sahih Muslim, Abu Dawud). Scholars explain it either as denying the ghoul altogether or as denying its power to change shape and mislead people at will.

title: God as Father
def: The Quran does not call God “Father”, to rule out the idea that He has children, but calls Him Lord, Merciful and Loving.
what: The Quran’s names for God include al-Raḥmān, al-Raḥīm, al-Wadūd (the Loving, 85:14) and al-Ghafūr. The Prophet said: “God is more merciful to His servants than a mother is to her child” (Sahih al-Bukhari), after seeing a mother searching for her lost baby.
misread: That in Islam God is distant and unloving.
sources: Islam avoids “Father” for God because of the Quran’s statement “He neither begets nor is begotten” (112:3), which excludes a literal fatherhood. The Bible itself uses “Father” also in a figurative sense of care. A believer in Islam speaks to God directly and with love: “say: if you love God, follow me, and God will love you” (3:31).

title: Gog and Magog
def: Two destructive peoples that the Quran says were walled off by Dhu al-Qarnayn, to break out near the end of time (18:94–99, 21:96).
what: People complained to Dhu al-Qarnayn that Gog and Magog were “corrupters on the earth”, and asked him to build a barrier. He built it of iron and molten copper and said: “This is a mercy from my Lord; when my Lord’s promise comes, He will make it level” (18:94–98). The Quran says that when they are released they will rush down from every height (21:96). A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari speaks of a breach in the wall, and one in Sahih Muslim of their emergence after the Dajjal.
sources: Ezekiel 38–39 and Revelation 20 also speak of Gog and Magog, and Muslims see this as part of a shared tradition of the end of time. Scholars differ on whether the wall is a historical structure, a figure for the barrier between order and chaos, or a reality of the unseen.

title: Goitein, S. D.
def: A Jewish historian (1900–1985) of the Cairo Geniza, author of A Mediterranean Society, a record of the medieval Jewish and Muslim world.
what: Shelomo Dov Goitein studied the documents of the Cairo Geniza and described the daily life of Jewish merchants, scholars and families in the Muslim Mediterranean between the tenth and thirteenth centuries. His study of the relations of Jews and Muslims, and his “Jews and Arabs”, are standard works.

title: Gold and silver
def: The Quran condemns hoarding gold and silver (9:34), and the Prophet forbade eating from vessels of gold or silver and gold ornaments for men.
what: “Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God’s way, give them tidings of a painful punishment” (9:34). The Prophet said that whoever drinks from vessels of gold and silver is gulping the fire of Hell into his belly (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim). He forbade gold and silk for men, and allowed them for women (Abu Dawud). The Quran describes Pharaoh’s boast: “why have no gold bracelets been given to him?” (43:53).

title: Golden calf
def: The calf the Israelites worshipped while Moses was on the mountain; in the Quran it was made by al-Samiri, not by Aaron.
what: The Quran says that after Moses left, his people took “a calf, a body with a lowing sound”, made of their ornaments (7:148, 20:88). It names al-Samiri as the one who led them to it (20:85, 20:95–97). Aaron warned them that they were being tested and told them to follow him (20:90). Moses rebuked the people and al-Samiri, burned the calf and scattered it in the sea (20:97).
sources: In the Quran it is Aaron who opposes the calf, and Moses’ anger at him (7:150) is that of a brother who feared he had not done enough. The Quran uses the story as an example of the Israelites’ readiness to fall back into idolatry, and of forgiveness after repentance (2:54).

title: Golden Rule
def: “None of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself” (hadith): the Muslim form of the rule of reciprocity.
what: The Prophet said: “None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself” (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim), and: “Whoever wishes to be saved from the Fire and to enter Paradise should die believing in God and the Last Day and treat people as he would like to be treated” (Sahih Muslim). The Quran asks believers to give what they would love (3:92).
sources: Jesus’ teaching in Matthew 7:12 and Rabbi Hillel’s negative form are the same principle, found in many traditions. Muslims see it as part of the ethics common to the prophets.

title: Goliath and Talut
def: The Quran’s story of David’s defeat of Goliath, in the kingship of Talut (Saul).
what: The Israelites asked their prophet for a king, and he told them “God has sent Talut as a king” (2:247). When Talut tested the army at a river, only a few obeyed (2:249). Those who did said: “How many a small company has overcome a large by God’s leave” (2:249). “David killed Goliath, and God gave him kingship and wisdom” (2:251).

title: Good
def: Islam says goodness belongs to God: “God is good and accepts only what is good” (hadith).
what: The Prophet said: “O people, God is good and accepts only what is good” (Sahih Muslim). The Quran calls God “the Beneficent” (52:28), and says that whatever good one has is from Him (16:53). Muslims also read Jesus’ words, “why do you call me good? No one is good but God alone” (Mark 10:18), as the teaching that only God is good in the absolute sense.

title: Grave
def: The Quran calls the time between death and resurrection a barrier (barzakh, 23:100), and burial is simple.
what: “Before them is a barrier (barzakh) until the day they are resurrected” (23:100). Hadith describe the questioning of the dead by two angels in the grave and ease or distress according to deeds (Sahih al-Bukhari). The Prophet prayed over the grave of a black woman who swept the mosque and whose death had gone unnoticed (Sahih al-Bukhari), and forbade building over graves. He permitted visiting graves, as a reminder of death (Sahih Muslim).

title: Greed and avarice
def: The Quran condemns miserliness and hoarding, and promises success to those saved from the greed of their own souls.
what: “Those who are stingy with what God has given them of His bounty should not think it good for them; it will be a burden on their necks on the Day of Resurrection” (3:180). Of those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God’s way, the Quran promises a painful punishment (9:34). “Whoever is saved from the greed of his own soul, those are the successful” (59:9).

title: Greeting non-Muslims
def: Hadith differ on greeting Christians and Jews first; the Prophet greeted mixed gatherings, and most scholars allow it.
what: The Quran says “when you are greeted with a greeting, answer with a better one, or return it” (4:86), and does not forbid kindness to those who have not fought the Muslims (60:8). A hadith in Sahih Muslim says not to greet the Jews and Christians first and to force them to the narrowest part of the road. Another, in Sahih al-Bukhari, says that the Prophet passed a gathering of Muslims, idolaters and Jews and greeted them all, and that when the People of the Book greet you, say “and upon you” (wa ʿalaykum).
sources: Scholars note that the first report came after the treachery of Banu Qurayza and was about a particular situation. Most jurists, including many of the Companions’ followers, allow greeting non-Muslims first, with Ibn Abbas and others reported to have done so. The Quran’s instruction to treat all with justice and kindness stands behind it.
